p01.part: the class must be a literal type with exactly one such conversion function
p01.why: Eight has two constexpr conversion functions to integer types, so it is not a valid alignas operand.

p02.part: an enumerator of a scoped enumeration is rejected
p02.why: Width::eight is an enumerator of a scoped enumeration.

p03.part: ORD-P1 row 'a call': only parameters with arguments take part; ORD-P2 step 6 tie-breakers 6c and 6d; ORD-P4 '6d needs parameter lists of the same length'
p03.why: Both templates compare as T against T, so each is at least as specialized; the ellipsis is not a pack for 6c, and 6d needs parameter lists of the same length, so neither wins and the call is ambiguous (doubtful: the model does not say how an ellipsis counts).

p04.part: OVL-P4 table row '<=>': (A, A) for every pair, reached through a conversion function; CMP-P5 result table; LSUP-P1 row '<=> on built-in operands'
p04.why: ToInt{} <=> 1 picks the built-in (int, int) and gives strong_ordering, ToDouble{} <=> 1.0 picks (double, double) and gives partial_ordering, and all three ordering classes are declared with their static members.

p05.part: SINIT-P2 table row 'a constant initializer, checked with constinit'; CE-P3 'A read of a scalar that has no value is rejected'
p05.why: The Holder constructor reads point.x before point is initialized, so the initializer is not a constant and constinit rejects it.

p06.part: DEFARG-P1 'a default argument that no call uses is never checked as a constant'
p06.why: No call uses the default argument, so the immediate call clamp(limit) is never checked.

p07.part: list item 'a member of a class template, which makes that member of every specialization a friend, and no other member'
p07.why: Only Box<T>::peek is a friend, so Box<int>::other cannot use the private secret.

p08.part: ORD-P1 rows 'a call with a member template' and 'a call with a swapped rewritten candidate'; ORD-P2 steps 3 and 6
p08.why: Both candidates are swapped member templates; W<T*> is more specialized than W<T>, so the one returning true wins.

p09.part: DEFARG-P1 'Each call that uses the default argument evaluates the immediate call there and rejects it when it is not a constant'
p09.why: pad() uses the default, and clamp(limit) reads the non-constant limit.

p10.part: LSUP-P1 table row '<=> on built-in operands' and 'a program that uses only <=> on two int values can declare std::strong_ordering with its static members'
p10.why: 4 <=> 9 gives strong_ordering::less, whose v is -1, so main returns 0.

p11.part: 'an initializer that reads a variable of scalar type from another unit can get its final value or zero'
p11.why: table_ready is either false, giving 0, or true after Table's constructor ran, giving 28; both make main return 0.

p12.part: ORD-P1 row 'a call with a swapped rewritten candidate' (parameters reversed) and the example note that GCC does not reverse the parameters (Q-0211); OVL-P3 order 2d before 2h
p12.why: With the reversal the swapped member template (T* const&) is more specialized and returns true, so Clang and EDG compile; GCC does not reverse, finds no order, picks the written candidate by 2h, which returns false, and rejects the static_assert.

p13.part: 'The class must be a literal type'; glossary 'literal type' needs an implicit, defaulted, or constexpr destructor
p13.why: W has a user-provided destructor that is not constexpr, so W is not a literal type and cannot give a bit-field width.

p14.part: ORD-P1 row 'an initialization by conversion function templates'; the example table row T& against const T&&
p14.why: Clang finds neither template more specialized and rejects; GCC and EDG choose T& and compile.

p15.part: 'The class must be a literal type with exactly one such conversion function'
p15.why: W has a destructor that is not constexpr, so W is not a literal type and cannot be an alignas operand.

p16.why: The values 1ULL << 63 and -1 need more than 64 bits, and no compiler has a wider type for the 32-bit target.

p17.part: the compiler table for a suffix that does not start with _ and that the language does not use
p17.why: GCC calls the literal operator and the program returns 0; Clang rejects 1u8 as an invalid suffix; EDG rejects because u8 starts with u.

p18.part: 'Two such lvalues of one class type are rejected.'
p18.why: const Box and volatile Box lvalues have cv-qualifier sets where neither includes the other.

p19.part: LSUP-P1 table row '<=> on built-in operands'
p19.why: 4 <=> 9 gives less, v is -1, so main returns 0.

p20.part: the compiler table for a suffix that does not start with _ and that the language does not use
p20.why: GCC calls the literal operator and the program returns 0; Clang rejects 1km; EDG calls the literal operator and accepts.

p21.part: DEFARG-P1 'the immediate function needs a definition only by that call'
p21.why: The call pad() comes after width is defined, so width() gives 3 and main returns 0.

p22.part: COND-P2 'If two class types each convert to the other, there is no single answer'; OVL-P1 'deletion ... come[s] into play only in step 4'
p22.why: Wrap converts to Tag through the deleted conversion function and Tag converts to Wrap through the constructor, so both directions convert and the expression is rejected (doubtful: the model does not say whether a deleted conversion counts).

p23.part: LSUP-P1 table, every row; the ordering classes are the page's own example
p23.why: Every part that each use needs is declared, and every assertion holds.

p24.part: the tuple protocol example for a class with a member get
p24.why: The program is the page's own example with a main; the bindings get 1, 5, 2, 7 and main returns 0.

p25.part: 'the function must be constexpr, because the conversion runs during constant evaluation'
p25.why: Eight's conversion function is not constexpr.

p26.part: 'a class that converts to one of these gives a size'
p26.why: Two converts to int, so the array has two elements; main returns 0.

p27.part: during constant evaluation 'a relational comparison of pointers to ... a base class subobject and a member' is rejected
p27.why: The static_assert evaluates the left operand of || first, and it orders a base subobject against a member.

p28.part: during constant evaluation 'a relational comparison of pointers to two base class subobjects of one object' is rejected
p28.why: The static_assert orders the Left and Right subobjects of both.

p29.part: 'a class type whose conversion function gives such a type ... literal type with exactly one such conversion function, and the function must be constexpr'
p29.why: Three meets every condition, so the width is 3.

p30.part: 'On x86-64, GCC uses a 128-bit integer type of its own ... Clang and EDG ... reject it.'
p30.why: GCC compiles; Clang and EDG reject.

p31.part: table row 'a defaulted <=>': the static members, a comparison of a value with 0 by == or !=
p31.why: strong_ordering has its static members and a != against int, which is enough for a defaulted <=> on two int members; the defaulted == checks the result.

p32.part: the operand conditions and 'alignas can make the alignment stricter'
p32.why: Eight has exactly one constexpr conversion to int, giving 8, which is a power of two and stricter than int's alignment.

p33.part: 'an enumerator of a scoped enumeration is rejected as a width'
p33.why: Bits::three belongs to a scoped enumeration.

p34.part: 'A suffix that the language uses keeps its built-in meaning, and the literal calls no literal operator', with the table of suffixes
p34.why: u, z, ll, f, and L are language suffixes, so no literal operator runs, calls stays 0, and main returns 0.

p35.part: CMP-P5 rejects 'a narrowing conversion' but no principle says whether int to double narrows; the glossary and CONV-P2 define narrowing as a conversion that 'can change a value', and int to double does not change any int value on x86-64
p35.why: The first two assertions hold through the built-in (int, long) and (int, int) candidates, but the principles leave open whether int <=> double is rejected as narrowing or gives partial_ordering.

p36.part: table row 'a defaulted <=>': a comparison of a value with 0 by == or !=
p36.why: strong_ordering has no == or != that takes 0, and its constructor is explicit, so the defaulted <=> cannot compare a part's result with 0.

p37.part: LSUP-P1 table row '<=> on built-in operands': the class it yields; CMP-P5 floating-point gives partial_ordering
p37.why: a <=> b on doubles yields std::partial_ordering, which the program does not declare.

p38.part: 'an enumerator of a scoped enumeration gives no size'

p39.why: W has two constexpr conversion functions to integer types.

p40.why: strong_ordering has its static members and == and != against int; Version{1,2} <=> Version{1,3} is less, so main returns 0.

p41.part: 'A declaration that names a member with a qualified name ... enters the scope of N at that name. The parts after the name see the members of N.'
p41.why: The body of shapes::Box finds length in shapes, so width is 2 and main returns 0.

p42.part: list item 'a member of a class template, which makes that member of every specialization a friend'
p42.why: Box<T>::peek and the member class Box<T>::Inner are friends for every T, so both reads of secret are allowed; 7 + 7 is 14 and main returns 0.

p43.part: 'An explicit specialization counts, so the member that it declares with the same name and type is a friend too'
p43.why: Box<char>::peek has the same name and type, so it may read secret; main returns 0.

p44.why: W's conversion function is not constexpr.
